LiteLLM CVE-2026-49468: Host header injection on protected management routes AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to LiteLLM management routes (/key, /user, /team, /model, /customer, /spend, /organization) where the Host header carries path/route tokens or control characters. CVE-2026-49468 abuses Starlette reconstructing request.url.path from the Host header, so an attacker injects route fragments into Host to make the auth gate evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. Rationale: Uses the exact LiteLLM management-route prefixes (corroborated via DeepWiki/docs) plus the article's stated root cause — Host header reconstructed into request.url.path — to flag Host values carrying path/route tokens or control chars, the literal injection mechanism. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this is an HTTP-header detection on a FastAPI web app; those telemetry sources carry no Host-header/route semantics. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/ • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse proxy/CDN appending X-Forwarded host data into a single Host field
  • Load balancer health-check probes using IP:port style Host values
  • Misconfigured client libraries sending full URLs as the Host header
  • Internal API gateway that rewrites Host with a routing prefix
  • Pentest/vuln-scanner activity from an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where not(HostHdr matches regex @"^[a-zA-Z0-9._\-]+(:\d{1,5})?$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request line for the flagged events — confirm the Host header genuinely contains route tokens or control chars (not just an odd-but-legit FQDN) and note the HTTP status returned. 2) Contain: if the proxy is directly internet-reachable, place it behind a CDN/WAF or reverse proxy with a server_name allowlist (per advisory workaround) and confirm/upgrade LiteLLM to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: from the same SrcIpAddr, pivot to all management-route requests, check for 200/201 responses and any /key/generate or /user/new actions that would indicate created keys or accounts to revoke.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| extend HostHdr = tostring(HttpHostName)
| where isnotempty(HostHdr)
// CVE-2026-49468: Host header is reconstructed into request.url.path; injection puts route tokens / control chars in Host
| where HostHdr matches regex @"[/\\;@]" or HostHdr has_any ("/key","/user","/team","/model","/customer","/spend","/organization","..","%2e")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HostHdr, HttpMethod, Url, StatusCode = toint(HttpStatusCode), HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM auth-bypass success: 401/403 then 200 to same management route (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Correlates failed auth (401/403) followed within 5 minutes by a successful (200/201/204) response to a LiteLLM management route from the same source. A fail-then-succeed sequence against protected /key, /user, /team, /model routes is the signature of a working Host-header auth bypass, especially when the Host header value changes between the two requests. Rationale: Targets the article's core impact (unauthenticated access to protected management routes) via a high-fidelity temporal shape: a rejected request immediately followed by a success on the same route/source, with Host-header divergence surfaced as the injection tell. Correlation + threshold means no Sigma; HTTP-only signal means Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch cannot express it. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/litellm/CVE-2026-49468/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin who mistyped/expired an API key, then retried with a valid one within 5 minutes
  • Token-refresh races where a client retries after a 401 with a renewed bearer token
  • Automation rotating keys that briefly 401s then succeeds
  • Load-balanced retries where the first node returns 401 due to cache lag
  • Authorized pentest replaying requests against the management API
Suppression filter
| where HostChanged == true or not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the matched pair — was the 200 served to a request lacking valid credentials, and did the Host header change between the 401 and the 200? A Host change is strong evidence of bypass. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF/proxy, force LiteLLM behind a Host-validating upstream, and upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate every management action that source performed after the success (key/user/team creation, model changes); rotate any keys created or exposed and review /spend and /user/list pulls for data access.
let win = 5m;
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
let fails = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (401, 403)
| project FailTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, FailUrl = Url, FailHost = tostring(HttpHostName);
let success = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SuccessUrl = Url, SuccessHost = tostring(HttpHostName), HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent;
fails
| join kind=inner success on SrcIpAddr
| where SuccessTime between (FailTime .. FailTime + win)
| extend HostChanged = FailHost != SuccessHost
| project FailTime, SuccessTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', SuccessTime, FailTime), SrcIpAddr, FailUrl, SuccessUrl, FailHost, SuccessHost, HostChanged, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by SuccessTime desc

LiteLLM rapid enumeration across multiple management-route categories (CVE-2026-49468) AIReconnaissance Medium
Flags a single source that successfully (200/201/204) hits 3+ distinct LiteLLM management-route categories (key/user/team/model/customer/spend/organization) within 10 minutes. Post-bypass exploitation of CVE-2026-49468 typically fans out across the management surface; legitimate admin activity usually stays within a narrow subset of routes. Rationale: Builds on the advisory's enumerated management surface (>14 routes across 7 categories, confirmed via LiteLLM DeepWiki) and treats breadth-of-access as the anomaly signal post-bypass. Threshold aggregation rules out Sigma; HTTP-route semantics rule out Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/public_routes
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM admin UI page load that fans out across several management endpoints in one session
  • Infrastructure-as-code/Terraform reconciliation touching keys, users, teams and models
  • Scheduled reporting job pulling /spend, /user/list and /key/list together
  • Onboarding automation that provisions a team, users and keys in sequence
  • Backup/export tooling iterating the full management API
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the source is the admin UI/IaC service account (expected) or an unrecognized/external IP; check whether the requests carried valid auth. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, block the source and restrict the proxy to internal networks plus a Host-validating upstream, then upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review state-changing calls in the burst (/key/generate, /user/new, /team/new, /model/new) and revoke artifacts created; correlate the same SrcIpAddr against the 401-then-200 detection to confirm bypass.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
| extend Category = extract(@"/(key|user|team|model|customer|spend|organization)/", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(Category)
| summarize Categories = make_set(Category), CategoryCount = dcount(Category), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hosts = make_set(HttpHostName, 10) by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CategoryCount >= 3   // 3+ distinct management categories in 10m = enumeration, not normal admin
| order by LastSeen desc

LiteLLM successful management-route access from external/unauthenticated source (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful (200/201/204) access to LiteLLM management routes that either carried no Authorization header or originated from a public (non-RFC1918) source IP. CVE-2026-49468 only works where the proxy is directly reachable without an upstream Host validator, so externally-sourced or credential-less successes on /key, /user, /team, /model routes are the direct expression of the bypass impact. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's central impact ("unauthenticated access to protected management routes") and its precondition (proxy directly reachable / no Host-normalizing upstream) using credential-less or public-source successes on the confirmed management routes. Higher FP rate where admins legitimately reach the API over the internet — pairs best with the 401-then-200 and enumeration UCs. HTTP-only signal, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://www.cryptika.com/critical-litellm-flaw-allows-authentication-bypass-via-host-header-injection/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin managing keys/users from a home or office public IP
  • CI/CD or SaaS automation calling the management API from a cloud egress IP
  • Logging pipeline that strips the Authorization header before forwarding (false 'no auth')
  • Monitoring/health checkers hitting management routes from external probes
  • Partner integration provisioning keys over the public internet
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog","Pingdom","UptimeRobot","GoogleHC")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is genuinely external/unexpected and that the 200 was served without valid credentials (account for log pipelines that drop the Authorization header). 2) Contain: place the proxy behind a CDN/WAF or reverse proxy with server_name allowlists, or restrict the listener to internal networks, and upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate all management actions from that source, rotate any keys returned by /key/generate or /key/info, audit /user/new and /team/new for rogue accounts, and review /spend output for data exposure.
let mgmt = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (mgmt)
| where toint(HttpStatusCode) in (200, 201, 204)
// successful management access with no Authorization header OR from a public (non-RFC1918) source
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) or (isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, IsPublic = iff(isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)), true, false), HasAuthHeader = isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization), HttpMethod, Url, HostHdr = tostring(HttpHostName), StatusCode = toint(HttpStatusCode), HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope

npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) AIInstallation High
Hunts a build/dev host resolving the trojanized easy-day-js dependency: the package landing under node_modules\easy-day-js, its setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the ~/.pkg_history / ~/.pkg_logs marker files the dropper writes to track installs. Article-specific because these exact filenames and the easy-day-js package path are the carrier injected into the @mastra scope. Rationale: Anchors on the exact carrier filenames named by Snyk and corroborated by Microsoft/StepSecurity: the easy-day-js node_modules path, setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs markers — none of which exist on a clean host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • Defenders deliberately caching the malicious tarball for IR/forensics
  • A renamed-but-unrelated package legitimately named easy-day-js in an internal registry mirror (rare)
  • Backup/EDR agents re-scanning an already-quarantined node_modules tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21/1.11.22 — check the project lockfile and whether npm install ran on/after 2026-06-17; pull the SHA256 of any setup.cjs found. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node-spawned detached process, and treat it as credential+wallet exposure — force-reset npm tokens, cloud creds, and browser-stored secrets used on that host; revoke/rotate any wallet seed phrases. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/.123 and persistence under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages; sweep CI runners and other dev laptops sharing the lockfile.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")) or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs") or TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000 AIDelivery High
Hunts the easy-day-js dropper's second-stage download: an outbound connection to the hardcoded Hostwinds host 23.254.164.92 on port 8000 (https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878), typically initiated by node.exe after TLS verification is disabled. High-fidelity because the IP+port are dedicated attacker infrastructure confirmed by multiple vendors. Rationale: Uses the verbatim dropper URL host/port (23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878) from the article; Microsoft and StepSecurity independently list this as the stage-2 download endpoint, so a hit is near-certainly the dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation of the sample making the same fetch
  • A blue-team connectivity test confirming the IOC is reachable/blocked
  • Shared NAT egress where another tool coincidentally targets the same /24 (verify exact IP+port)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — a node.exe/npm child reaching this IP confirms dropper execution; capture the host, user, and the resolved second-stage file in %TEMP%. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and treat as credential+wallet compromise (rotate dev/cloud/npm tokens, browser secrets). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to 23.254.164.123 beacons and C:\ProgramData\NodePackages persistence; block the full 23.254.164.0/24 Hostwinds range pending review.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92" and RemotePort == 8000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.92" and DstPortNumber == 8000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the second-stage crypto-stealer/RAT beaconing to its C2 at 23.254.164.123 roughly every 10 minutes over a self-signed wolfSSL channel. Aggregates repeat connections per host to surface the sustained beacon cadence rather than a single hit, distinguishing it from the one-shot dropper download. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RAT C2 IP (23.254.164.123) and the ~10-minute beacon described; the count>=3 aggregation captures the sustained cadence and filters single stray probes. No Sigma emitted because the detection is a threshold/aggregation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/IR detonation of the stealer producing repeat beacons
  • Security tooling actively probing the IOC for reachability
  • Another host in the same /24 being contacted for unrelated reasons (pin to exact IP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm beacon cadence and the originating process; a ~10-min periodic connection from a non-browser process is the RAT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 23.254.164.123 at egress, and snapshot memory before reimage; treat all secrets entered on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: enumerate persistence (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages on Windows, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nvm.protocal.plist on macOS, ~/.config/systemd/user/nvmconf.service on Linux) and check other hosts beaconing to the same /24.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 5), Proc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
            Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 5) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:23.254.164.123
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.123"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 3

| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the cross-platform persistence the stealer installs while disguised as Node tooling: Windows staging under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, macOS LaunchAgent com.nvm.protocal.plist, and Linux systemd user service nvmconf.service. Article-specific because these exact persistence names are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-unique persistence names from the article (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service) — the misspelled 'protocal' and 'nvmconf' are distinctive enough that a hit is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the persistence file content points to a NodePackages-staged payload or beacon; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: remove the LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Run entry, kill the persisted process, isolate the host, and rotate all credentials/wallets used there. 3) Hunt: correlate with 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and the easy-day-js install artifacts on the same and peer hosts; sweep all OS types since persistence is cross-platform.

Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated cross-platform crypto-stealer/RAT second stage by file hash on both write and execution. Hash matching is resilient to IP/infra rotation and is effectively zero-FP; the primary hash (221c45...) is the article-named stage-2 payload corroborated by Microsoft. Rationale: Primary hash 221c45a7... is the article-named second-stage payload and is corroborated by Microsoft Threat Intelligence; the additional campaign hashes are bundled IOCs. Hash matching is zero-FP and survives infrastructure rotation, complementing the IP-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox host where the sample was intentionally executed
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy retaining the hash on disk
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: any hit is high-confidence malicious — confirm host, user, and whether the hash was written vs executed; the payload self-deletes, so a FileWrite without a later process may indicate cleanup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and treat as full credential+wallet compromise — rotate cloud/npm/dev secrets and assume browser-stored wallet data exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and NodePackages/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence; submit the hash to org-wide retro-hunt across EDR.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_hash="221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf" OR Filesystem.file_hash="b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4" OR Filesystem.file_hash="c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638" OR Filesystem.file_hash="cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066" OR Filesystem.file_hash="9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposed vulnerable LobeHub instance <=2.1.56 (CVE-2026-54157) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST to LobeHub /webapi/proxy from scripted/CLI User-Agent (CVE-2026-54157 SSRF) · [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy reflected Set-Cookie injection of Clerk session cookies · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-54157: LobeHub: Unauthenticated SSRF in `/webapi/prox
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] LobeHub server process outbound connections to metadata/internal IPs (SSRF egress confirmation)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting internal/loopback IP ranges in POST body · [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting cloud metadata or internal service ports
Unauthenticated POST to LobeHub /webapi/proxy from scripted/CLI User-Agent (CVE-2026-54157 SSRF) AIExploitation High
Hunts direct exploitation of the unauthenticated SSRF in LobeHub's /webapi/proxy endpoint. The article's PoC is a raw curl POST with a text/plain body; legitimate proxy traffic only originates from the LobeHub browser UI, so a POST to this exact path from curl/wget/python-requests/PowerShell is high-fidelity exploitation against a self-hosted LobeHub (<=2.1.56). Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint (/webapi/proxy), method (POST), and the curl-based PoC, plus the fact that every other webapi route requires checkAuth() so legit proxy traffic is browser-only. Cross-checked vs lobehub/lobe-chat#9643 which independently names the same unauthenticated endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://github.com/lobehub/lobe-chat/issues/9643 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal monitoring/synthetic checks (Datadog, UptimeRobot) probing the endpoint after the advisory
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus) running the CVE-2026-54157 template
  • Security team reproducing the PoC with curl during validation
  • A custom internal integration that legitimately calls the proxy via a server-side HTTP client
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake","GoogleHC","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog/Synthetics")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP and the full request; confirm the path is exactly /webapi/proxy and method POST. Check whether the LobeHub instance version is <=2.1.56 and internet-exposed. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, block the source IP at the WAF/edge and apply the fix (wrap the route in checkAuth() or remove the endpoint). Rotate Clerk session secrets if cookie reflection is suspected. 3) Hunt: review all POSTs to /webapi/proxy for the same source over 30 days, look for internal-IP/metadata targets (see related UCs) and any reflected Set-Cookie responses.
let scriptedUA = dynamic(["curl","Wget","python-requests","python-urllib","Go-http-client","PowerShell","libwww-perl","okhttp","Java/","axios","node-fetch","HTTPie","Nuclei","Nmap"]);

| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem =~ "/webapi/proxy"
| where UserAgent has_any (scriptedUA)
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsMethod, CsUriStem, UserAgent, ScStatus, CsBytes, ScBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting internal/loopback IP ranges in POST body AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SSRF probing of internal networks through the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy. The endpoint fetches any URL supplied in the POST body server-side, so a body referencing loopback (127.0.0.1), RFC1918 ranges, or file://-style schemes indicates an attacker using LobeHub's infra to reach internal services. Requires a WAF/reverse-proxy that logs request bodies. Rationale: Builds on the article's statement that the proxy 'accepts a URL in the POST body and fetches it server-side without any authentication' (CVE-2024-32964 redirect-bypass history shows internal-network reach was the original impact). The internal-IP regex on the logged target URL is the article-specific SSRF signature; FP-prone because it depends on WAF body logging and benign internal previews. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate URL-preview of an internal wiki/Confluence link a user pasted into LobeHub
  • WAF inspecting a body that merely mentions an RFC1918 IP in unrelated text
  • Internal pen-test / red-team validating the SSRF
  • Developer testing the proxy against localhost during deployment
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Mozilla","Chrome","Safari","Edg/") and Message has "intranet-preview")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the POST body, confirm the fetched URL resolves to an internal/loopback target and that the response was returned (ScStatus 200). 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, patch LobeHub (checkAuth on /webapi/proxy) and restrict egress from the LobeHub host to internal ranges. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct internal target the source attempted, correlate to network-layer egress from the LobeHub node process (see network-egress UC) to confirm which internal services were actually reached.

| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where Message matches regex @"(?i)(127\.0\.0\.\d{1,3}|localhost|0\.0\.0\.0|\bfile://|\bgopher://|\bdict://|10\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}|192\.168\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}|172\.(1[6-9]|2\d|3[01])\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3})"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting cloud metadata or internal service ports AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-theft escalation of CVE-2026-54157: a /webapi/proxy POST body pointing at the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) or internal datastore ports (Redis 6379, etcd 2379, Mongo 27017, Postgres 5432). On a self-hosted LobeHub running on a cloud VM with IMDSv1, this returns instance-role credentials. Includes a CloudTrail escalation query for stolen-credential reuse. Rationale: Maps the article's stated impact ('use LobeHub's infrastructure ... abusing IP-based trust') to the canonical SSRF-to-IMDS escalation. 169.254.169.254/metadata.google.internal in a proxy body is never legitimate for a chat app. The CloudWatch query surfaces EC2 instance-role credentials (session name = instance-id i-...) used from a non-internal IP, the hallmark of IMDS credential theft if LobeHub runs on EC2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team validating IMDS reachability through the SSRF
  • Legitimate AssumedRole sessions from a corporate NAT egress IP not in RFC1918 (refine with your known egress CIDRs)
  • SSM/Session-Manager workflows assuming an instance role from an allow-listed bastion
  • WAF flagging a body that references a metadata IP in a non-fetch context
Suppression filter
| where not isPresent(errorCode)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the proxy body targeted 169.254.169.254/metadata and the response body (returned by the proxy) contained credential material or IAM role JSON. 2) Contain: immediately revoke/rotate the instance role's session credentials, enforce IMDSv2 (hop-limit 1, token required), block the attacker IP, and patch /webapi/proxy. 3) Hunt: run the CloudTrail query for the instance-role session name (i-...) used from any external IP in the last 30 days; review S3/STS/IAM actions performed by that session for data access.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where Message has_any ("169.254.169.254","metadata.google.internal","100.100.100.200",":6379",":2379",":27017",":5432",":9200",":8500",":2375")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName
| filter userIdentity.type = "AssumedRole"
  and userIdentity.arn like /:assumed-role\/.+\/i-[0-9a-f]+$/
  and sourceIPAddress not like /^(10\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)/
  and sourceIPAddress != "AWS Internal"
| sort @timestamp desc

LobeHub /webapi/proxy reflected Set-Cookie injection of Clerk session cookies AIExploitation High
Hunts the session-fixation primitive in CVE-2026-54157: the proxy passes upstream Set-Cookie headers straight through, so a POST body whose target reflects a Set-Cookie for Clerk's __session/__clerk_db_jwt/__client_uat cookies scoped to Domain=lobehub.com plants a known session value on victims. The cookie-injection payload appears verbatim in the request body. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's cookie-injection PoC: the body contains Set-Cookie + the Clerk cookie names (__session/__clerk_db_jwt/__client_uat, confirmed via Clerk docs) + Domain=lobehub.com. That triad in a /webapi/proxy body is unambiguous exploitation; no benign request reflects auth cookies through the proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://clerk.com/docs/guides/how-clerk-works/cookies
ATT&CKT1539 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the session-fixation PoC
  • A legitimate upstream that genuinely sets a __session cookie being previewed (rare; still worth investigating)
  • WAF body inspection matching the cookie name inside unrelated documentation text
  • Internal QA testing Clerk cookie behaviour through the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full Set-Cookie value from the body, note the planted __session value and victim scope (Domain=lobehub.com). 2) Contain: invalidate all Clerk sessions / rotate session signing keys so the fixed value is unusable, patch /webapi/proxy (checkAuth), and add a WAF rule stripping reflected Set-Cookie from proxy responses. 3) Hunt: identify any user who authenticated shortly after this request (session fixation completes at victim login) and force re-auth; review for CSRF auto-submit referers in the access logs.

| where Message has "Set-Cookie"
| where Message has_any ("__session","__clerk_db_jwt","__client_uat")
| where Message has "lobehub.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LobeHub server process outbound connections to metadata/internal IPs (SSRF egress confirmation) AICommand & Control Medium
Network-layer confirmation that CVE-2026-54157 SSRF reached internal infrastructure: the LobeHub Node server process initiating connections to the cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) or internal RFC1918 hosts it would never normally contact. Excludes LobeHub's legitimate local-LLM (Ollama) and database ports to keep signal high. Rationale: Corroborates SSRF success at the network layer: a LobeHub Node process reaching 169.254.169.254 or internal hosts is anomalous for a chat app. Port exclusions (11434 Ollama, 5432 Postgres, 6379 Redis, etc.) remove LobeHub's own legitimate backend traffic so internal-probing/metadata hits stand out. Scoped via the node process + 'lobe' command-line/path hint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964
ATT&CKT1046 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LobeHub legitimately calling a self-hosted Ollama/vLLM/LM Studio on a non-excluded internal port
  • LobeHub server contacting an internal Postgres/Redis on a non-standard port
  • Container health-checks or service-mesh sidecars from the Node process
  • A self-hosted internal LLM gateway on RFC1918 that the deployment legitimately uses
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIPType in ("Private","Loopback") and RemotePort in (11434,1234,8000,5432,6379))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Node process is the LobeHub server and the internal/metadata destination is not a sanctioned backend (LLM/DB). For 169.254.169.254, treat as credential-theft attempt immediately. 2) Contain: restrict egress from the LobeHub host (deny RFC1918 + link-local except sanctioned backends), enforce IMDSv2, patch /webapi/proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound /webapi/proxy POSTs on the same host/time to recover the exact attacker-supplied target URL; rotate any credentials reachable at the contacted internal service.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","next-server","bun.exe","bun","deno.exe","deno")
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("metadata.google.internal","metadata.goog")
    or (RemoteIPType in ("Private","Loopback","LinkLocal")
        and RemotePort !in (11434,1234,8000,5000,3000,8080,11435,5432,6379,6333,27017)
        and (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "lobe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "lobe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, RemoteIPType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254"
    or DstHostname has "metadata.google.internal"
    or (ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) and DstPortNumber !in (11434,1234,8000,5000,3000,8080,5432,6379,6333,27017))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed vulnerable LobeHub instance <=2.1.56 (CVE-2026-54157) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-exposure detection for self-hosted LobeHub running an affected version (npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56) carrying the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy SSRF. Surfaces vulnerable, potentially internet-facing instances from the vulnerability inventory so they can be patched before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete affected-package facts: CVE-2026-54157 and npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56. The Defender query joins DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to prioritise exposed instances (the SSRF is unauthenticated, so internet-facing is critical). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@lobehub/lobehub/CVE-2026-54157/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lagging on a host already patched to >2.1.56 (stale inventory)
  • Air-gapped/internal-only LobeHub instances flagged as critical despite no internet exposure
  • A pinned fork that backported the checkAuth fix while reporting an old version string
  • Dev/test LobeHub container images not in production
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running LobeHub version and whether the instance is internet-facing (IsInternetFacing/PublicIP). 2) Contain: patch to a fixed release (>2.1.56) or apply the checkAuth() wrapper / remove /webapi/proxy; place behind authenticated reverse-proxy if patch is delayed. 3) Hunt: for any instance confirmed exposed, retro-hunt its web logs for /webapi/proxy POSTs (see exploitation UCs) to determine if it was already abused before patching.

    or (SoftwareVendor has "lobehub" and SoftwareName has_any ("lobehub","lobe-chat","lobe chat"))

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

Crawl4AI /screenshot or /pdf output_path traversal → arbitrary file write outside output dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the CWE-22 arbitrary-file-write in Crawl4AI's /screenshot and /pdf endpoints, where an unvalidated output_path lets an attacker drop files outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs. Detects the crawl4ai server process (python/uvicorn/gunicorn) creating files in sensitive locations (cron, .ssh, shell rc files, /etc, /root) it should never write to. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf), the named safe directory (/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs), and the server process identity. A web crawler writing to cron/.ssh/.bashrc is near-zero-FP. Datadog left empty — provided linux.auditd schema lacks a target-file-path field. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI configured with a custom CRAWL4AI_OUTPUT_DIR pointing at /app or /usr/local (operator misconfig)
  • Admin/CI process running inside the container as the same python interpreter doing legitimate package installs into /usr/local
  • Browser engine (chromium) writing cache under /home/appuser/.cache if process attribution rolls up to python
  • Init/entrypoint scripts seeding config into /app on first boot
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/usr/local/lib/python" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip","setup.py","wheel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full FolderPath/FileName and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the write landed outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs and inspect the dropped file's content (web shell, cron entry, authorized_keys). Correlate with web logs for the /screenshot or /pdf request carrying output_path. 2) Contain: isolate the container/host, kill the crawl4ai worker, and revoke any keys/creds present in the written path; if a cron or authorized_keys entry was added, remove it. 3) Hunt: search all crawl4ai hosts for other writes outside the output dir, and pivot on the source IP across /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js. Upgrade Crawl4AI to >=0.8.7.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn)$"
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(python|uvicorn|gunicorn)"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/","/root/","/etc/cron","/.ssh","authorized_keys","/.bashrc","/.profile","/usr/local/","/app/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI SSRF: crawler process reaching cloud-metadata or RFC1918 internal IPs AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the SSRF chain across Crawl4AI's /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js and webhook endpoints (CWE-918), where attacker-supplied URLs make the server fetch internal services and the 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata endpoint — including the IPv6-mapped bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Flags the crawl4ai/browser process connecting to metadata or private ranges, which a public-web crawler should never do. Rationale: Cloud-metadata IP 169.254.169.254 (and its ::ffff: mapped form, the CVE-2026-53754 bypass) is essentially never a legitimate destination for a public-web crawler, making it a high-fidelity SSRF anchor; RFC1918 hits are the broader hunting tier. Process-scoped to the named crawl4ai runtimes. CloudWatch left empty — IMDS access is host-network, not visible in CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately connecting to an internal Redis (6379) / Postgres (5432) backend on the Docker bridge network
  • Crawl4AI calling a self-hosted LLM/embedding endpoint on a private IP (Ollama, vLLM)
  • Health-check or service-mesh sidecar traffic from the same container to private ranges
  • Crawling an explicitly allowed internal staging site during QA
Suppression filter
| where not (RemotePort in (6379, 5432, 11434) and not MetadataHit)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination — a hit on 169.254.169.254 is a confirmed SSRF/credential-theft attempt; for RFC1918 hits, check RemotePort/RemoteUrl and whether it matches a known internal service. Pull the matching /crawl, /md, /llm or webhook request from web logs. 2) Contain: if metadata was reached, rotate the instance role / IMDS credentials immediately and enforce IMDSv2 (hop limit 1); block the source IP and disable /execute_js (CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED). 3) Hunt: review CloudTrail/Activity logs for any API calls made with the instance role shortly after the metadata hit, and pivot on the source IP for internal-range fan-out (port scanning). Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|chromium|chrome|headless_shell|node)$"
| extend MetadataHit = (RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteIP == "::ffff:169.254.169.254")
| where MetadataHit or ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP) or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "169.254.0.0/16")
| extend Severity = iff(MetadataHit, "CRITICAL-cloud-metadata", "internal-SSRF")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Severity

Crawl4AI /execute_js sandbox escape: crawler/browser process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts the arbitrary-JavaScript-execution / hook-sandbox-escape vulnerability (CWE-94) in Crawl4AI's /execute_js endpoint, where attacker JS (or the asyncio/hook bypass) breaks out to OS command execution. Detects the python/uvicorn/gunicorn server or its headless-chromium/node children spawning an interactive shell — behaviour a web crawler never exhibits. Rationale: Process-tree pivot on the article's named runtime (python/uvicorn/gunicorn + the playwright headless-chromium it drives) spawning a shell directly maps the /execute_js RCE and hook sandbox-escape outcome. Datadog left empty — the provided linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent→child constraint cannot be expressed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately shelling out to a PDF/image post-processing tool (wkhtmltopdf, ghostscript) via subprocess
  • Container entrypoint or healthcheck script invoking sh from the gunicorn master
  • Operator running 'docker exec ... bash' attributed to the server process tree
  • A debugging hook intentionally enabled in non-prod that runs shell commands
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wkhtmltopdf","ghostscript","/usr/bin/gs","libreoffice") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — benign post-processing (ghostscript/wkhtmltopdf) vs reverse shell / curl|sh / recon (id, uname, whoami). Correlate timing with a POST to /execute_js in web logs. 2) Contain: kill the shell and parent worker, isolate the container, and disable /execute_js via CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false (and remove --disable-web-security if present). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to UC2 (SSRF egress) and UC1 (file writes), and search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound C2 from the shell PID. Upgrade to >=0.8.7.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(python[0-9.]*|uvicorn|gunicorn|node|chromium|chrome|headless_shell)$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|ash)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI unauthenticated access to /monitor endpoints (auth bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CWE-306 missing-authentication flaw where Crawl4AI's monitor router was mounted without token_dep, exposing destructive endpoints like /monitor/actions/cleanup and the /monitor/ws WebSocket with no auth. Detects successful requests to /monitor paths that carry no Authorization header. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable paths (/monitor/actions/cleanup, /monitor/ws) plus the auth-bypass signature — a successful response with an empty Authorization header. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this needs HTTP request-header visibility that only the reverse-proxy/WAF (Sentinel ImWebSession / CIM Web) carries; Sigma skipped because 'webserver' is outside the allowed logsource categories. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal monitoring/uptime check polling /monitor without a token (pre-patch, by design)
  • An ops dashboard reverse-proxy that strips the Authorization header before the app tier (header invisible to upstream logger)
  • Health probes from Kubernetes/Docker hitting /monitor/* and returning 200
  • Internal load-balancer keep-alive traffic to the monitor WebSocket
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog","Pingdom"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the request reached a destructive endpoint (/monitor/actions/cleanup) vs read-only monitor views, and whether the source IP is internal/expected. Check for a burst of /monitor/* enumeration from one IP. 2) Contain: put the monitor router behind auth (deploy >=0.8.7 / set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN) and restrict network access to the Docker API; block the offending source IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: from the same source IP, pivot to /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js and /crawl activity (UC1/UC2/UC3/UC5) and review whether cleanup actually deleted job/output data.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/monitor/"
| where Url has_any ("/monitor/actions/cleanup","/monitor/actions","/monitor/ws","/monitor/")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","101","204")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/monitor/actions/cleanup*","*/monitor/actions*","*/monitor/ws*","*/monitor/*")) AND Web.status IN ("200","101","204") by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/monitor/actions/cleanup*","*/monitor/actions*","*/monitor/ws*","*/monitor/*")) AND Web.status IN ("200","101","204") by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Crawl4AI web-payload abuse: path traversal, XSS, file:// and metadata-IP in crawl requests AIDelivery Medium
Hunts malicious payloads sent to Crawl4AI's exposed endpoints (/screenshot, /pdf, /crawl, /md, /llm, /execute_js, /markdown_extraction, /llm_extraction): output_path traversal sequences, stored-XSS markup (CWE-79), file:// LFI URLs, and literal cloud-metadata / IPv6-mapped targets used for SSRF. A single web-log pivot that surfaces exploitation attempts before they succeed. Rationale: Combines the article's full endpoint inventory with concrete exploit signatures it names: output_path traversal, XSS markup, the file:// LFI vector (VulnCheck-confirmed) and the ::ffff: IPv6-mapped metadata bypass (CVE-2026-53754). Hunting tier because many payloads ride in POST bodies that not all proxies log into the URL field — pairs with the behavioural UCs (1/2/3) for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53754/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate crawl target whose URL genuinely contains '../' in its query string or path
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Burp, Nuclei) probing the endpoints during authorized testing
  • A crawled page URL that legitimately references file:// in a parameter value
  • Crawling a security blog whose URL contains '<script' or 'onerror=' as article-content text
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nuclei","Burp","sqlmap","Nessus") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: classify the payload type (traversal vs XSS vs file:// vs metadata-IP) and check the HTTP status — a 200 on /screenshot+output_path traversal or /crawl+file:// suggests success. Cross-reference the source IP with UC1/UC2/UC3 host telemetry for an actual file write, SSRF egress, or shell. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, disable /execute_js, and ensure the patched SSRF/path validators are deployed (>=0.8.7). 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct payload that IP sent across all endpoints, and confirm whether any stored XSS persisted in the monitor dashboard (escapeHtml present?).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/screenshot","/pdf","/crawl","/md","/llm","/execute_js","/markdown_extraction","/llm_extraction")
| where Url has_any ("../","..%2f","..%2F","%2e%2e","<script","onerror=","onclick=","onload=","file://","169.254.169.254","::ffff:","metadata.google.internal","output_path=")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/screenshot*","*/pdf*","*/crawl*","*/md*","*/llm*","*/execute_js*","*/markdown_extraction*","*/llm_extraction*")) AND (Web.url IN ("*../*","*..%2f*","*%2e%2e*","*<script*","*onerror=*","*onclick=*","*file://*","*169.254.169.254*","*::ffff:*","*metadata.google*","*output_path=*")) by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*/screenshot*","*/pdf*","*/crawl*","*/md*","*/llm*","*/execute_js*","*/markdown_extraction*","*/llm_extraction*")) AND (Web.url IN ("*../*","*..%2f*","*%2e%2e*","*<script*","*onerror=*","*onclick=*","*file://*","*169.254.169.254*","*::ffff:*","*metadata.google*","*output_path=*")) by Web.src Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
