Crawl4AI CVE-2026-53753 sandbox-escape payload (gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins) in POST /crawl body AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of the Crawl4AI Docker API AST sandbox escape by matching the frame-introspection chain (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins, __import__) inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy computed-field expression POSTed to /crawl. These Python generator/frame attribute names have zero benign reason to appear in crawl-extraction schemas, making them a high-fidelity exploit signature. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim exploit primitives gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins/__import__ plus the JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema key and the /crawl endpoint. The frame-attribute chain is the literal sandbox-escape technique named by the advisory and has no benign occurrence in extraction schemas. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory Database (CVSS 9.8, fixed 0.8.7) which confirms the gi_frame.f_back computed-field eval() escape. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / pentest tooling (Nuclei, Burp) replaying the public PoC against an internal Crawl4AI instance during authorised testing
  • Internal red-team validation of the patch on a staging Crawl4AI container
  • A developer pasting the advisory PoC into a request while reproducing the bug for the 0.8.7 upgrade
  • WAF that mirrors blocked-request bodies into the same log index (action=blocked rows — still worth reviewing but not a live compromise)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","reset")  // keep only requests that actually reached the app; drop WAF-blocked replays during triage tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the SourceIP+RequestClientApplication; confirm the body carries a gi_frame/f_back chain inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema, and check the running Crawl4AI version (<=0.8.6 vulnerable) and whether CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN/JWT auth is set. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, remove the container from public network exposure, and rotate any secrets the container can reach (env vars, mounted files, instance role). 3) Hunt: on the affected host run the post-RCE process-tree and credential-enumeration detections from first-seen time, and review egress from the uvicorn/python process to attacker infrastructure.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/crawl"
| where Message has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","JsonCssExtractionStrategy","__import__")
   or RequestContext has_any ("gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","__import__")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
(sourcetype="*nginx*" OR sourcetype="*apache*" OR sourcetype="*waf*" OR sourcetype="*proxy*") "/crawl" ("gi_frame" OR "f_back" OR "f_builtins" OR "JsonCssExtractionStrategy" OR "__import__")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by host, source, sourcetype, clientip
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Crawl4AI/uvicorn post-RCE: Python web service spawning shell or recon binaries AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-53753: the Crawl4AI Python/uvicorn/gunicorn process spawning interactive shells (sh, bash, dash) or reconnaissance utilities (curl, wget, nc, socat, whoami, id, uname). A crawler web service has no legitimate reason to fork these, so this is a high-confidence signal that the AST sandbox escape achieved code execution. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated impact ('execute arbitrary system commands') by pivoting on the exact server stack named in the advisory (Crawl4AI Docker API served by uvicorn/Python) spawning shells or recon tools — a tree that never occurs in normal crawler operation. The pip/pytest/playwright exclusion strips the only routine python-spawns-shell cases. Corroborated via GitLab GLAD entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Container build/CI steps where python runs 'pip install' which forks sh (covered by the filter)
  • Crawl4AI/Playwright bootstrapping that shells out to install browser dependencies on first run
  • A devops entrypoint script that uses python to wrap curl/wget for healthchecks
  • Operator debugging the container interactively via 'docker exec' producing python->bash (verify it was a human shell, not the web worker)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install","conda")) and AccountName !in~ ("root")  // optionally drop root-context build steps if the service runs as a non-root crawl user
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the parent uvicorn/python tree; confirm this is the Crawl4AI web worker (not a CI/pip/playwright bootstrap or an interactive docker exec). 2) Contain: isolate the container/host from the network, kill the offending process tree, and snapshot the container filesystem and memory for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to the /crawl WAF detection to find the originating exploit request, and to the credential-enumeration detection to see whether secrets or the metadata endpoint were touched; review all egress from the worker process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","whoami","id","uname")
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","pytest","jupyter","playwright install"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI post-RCE credential & cloud-metadata enumeration via Python-spawned subprocess AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts post-exploitation credential theft following CVE-2026-53753: a Crawl4AI Python/shell process reading /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, the process environment (/proc/self/environ, printenv), or the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254). The advisory explicitly calls out 'exfiltrate secrets', and a web crawler reaching these paths is a strong indicator the sandbox escape was used to harvest credentials. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's 'read/write files, and exfiltrate secrets' impact statement and the listed T1552.001 technique. Anchors the well-known secret targets (/etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, IMDS 169.254.169.254) to the Crawl4AI Python/shell parent chain so it fires on attacker harvesting rather than routine admin reads. Corroborated via the GitLab Advisory Database entry for CVE-2026-53753. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/CVE-2026-53753/ • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.005 T1083 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A container entrypoint/healthcheck script reading /etc/passwd to resolve a uid before dropping privileges
  • Legitimate app code calling printenv/env for config diagnostics under the python worker
  • Monitoring agents (Datadog/aws-otel) querying 169.254.169.254 for instance identity — verify the parent is the agent, not the crawl worker
  • An operator running 'cat /etc/passwd' via docker exec while troubleshooting (interactive, not web-worker-spawned)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("datadog-agent","aws-otel-collector","cloud-init")) and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("getent passwd","id -u"))  // drop monitoring agents and benign uid lookups while keeping shadow/environ/IMDS reads
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which secret was touched (/etc/shadow vs environ vs IMDS) and confirm the parent chain traces to the Crawl4AI uvicorn/python worker rather than a sidecar/monitoring agent; check whether 169.254.169.254 actually returned IAM/role credentials. 2) Contain: rotate every credential reachable from the container — env-var secrets, mounted files, and any cloud instance-profile/role credentials — and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: in CloudTrail, search for AssumeRole and API activity using the container's instance-profile role from new source IPs since first-seen, and pivot to the /crawl exploit and shell-spawn detections to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or FileName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","sh","bash","dash")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","/proc/self/environ","/proc/self/cmdline","169.254.169.254","latest/meta-data")
   or TargetProcessName in~ ("printenv","env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple JetBrains IDE plugins caught stealing AI keys

Aikido
2026-06-16 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A coordinated campaign of at least 15 JetBrains IDE plugins, published under seven vendor accounts, exfiltrates the AI provider API key you paste into their settings. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

IPs39.107.60.51

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE plugin AI-key exfil: endpoint egress to C2 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any host making an outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 39.107.60.51 used by 15 trojanized JetBrains Marketplace plugins (DeepSeek/CodeGPT clones) to ship stolen OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys. The connection is initiated by the JetBrains IDE JVM the instant a user clicks Apply on the plugin settings, so the process context is a Java/JetBrains runtime, not a browser. Rationale: Anchored on the single hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 (verbatim from the article's network-call code block, defanged 39.107.60[.]51) — a dedicated attacker host with no legitimate use, cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News. Any connection is dispositive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-ai.html • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher/sandbox detonating one of the named plugins to reproduce the IOC
  • Threat-intel or attack-surface scanners (Shodan/Censys) probing the IP from a corporate egress
  • IP reuse: the Alibaba Cloud address later reassigned to a benign tenant (validate WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • A SOAR/enrichment playbook auto-resolving or pinging the IOC and generating an event
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess is a JetBrains runtime (idea64.exe/pycharm64.exe/java/jetbrains-runtime) and pull the user; enumerate that user's installed JetBrains plugins against the 15 named IDs. 2) Contain: treat every AI provider API key (OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow) entered on that host as compromised — revoke and rotate immediately, uninstall the plugin, and block 39.107.60.51 at egress. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for the IP, and pivot to UC 'malicious JetBrains plugin install' to find dormant infections that haven't yet phoned home.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName,
          SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL,
          ApplicationProtocol, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains AI-key stealer HTTP exfil: cleartext POST to /api/software/ path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the application-layer signature of the theft in web-proxy/network-sensor telemetry: a plaintext HTTP POST to the URI path /api/software/<name> carrying the victim's API key as JSON. This survives C2 IP rotation by keying on the distinctive hardcoded URL path, and catches IDE traffic that egresses through a proxy where EDR socket attribution is weak. Rationale: Uses two verbatim article strings — the URL path /api/software/ from the network-call code block and the C2 IP 39.107.60.51 — over plaintext HTTP (article: 'reached over plain HTTP'). The path keys the detection independently of the IP. Datadog/Falcon left empty: standard FDR network events and the listed Datadog sources don't carry HTTP URI paths, so this needs proxy/web-gateway telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fifteen-jetbrains-marketplace/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal/SaaS API that legitimately exposes a '/api/software/' inventory endpoint reached over HTTP
  • Software-asset-management or patch agents POSTing to a vendor '/api/software/' path
  • Web-app vulnerability scanners fuzzing '/api/' routes from a corporate host
  • Proxy replay/cached events double-counting the same flow
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51" or Url has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full request — confirm the host header/destination resolves to 39.107.60.51 and, if PCAP/full-proxy is available, look for the static header X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing an 'sk-' key. 2) Contain: rotate/revoke the leaked provider key(s), remove the offending JetBrains plugin, and add both the IP and the URI path as egress-block + proxy-deny rules. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for any other host hitting /api/software/ (catches infections after a C2 IP change) and correlate with the endpoint-egress UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "HttpConnectionInspected"
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/software/" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (Url has "/api/software/" or DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51")
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install (15 DeepSeek/CodeGPT clone IDs) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts on-disk presence or install of any of the 15 trojanized JetBrains plugins by matching their Marketplace display names under a JetBrains \plugins\ directory. Covers the initial-access/supply-chain step and surfaces dormant infections on hosts that haven't yet entered an API key or phoned home to the C2. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim list of 15 malicious plugin display names installed under JetBrains \plugins\ paths — the supply-chain delivery artifact. Hunting-tier because the 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone name overlaps the legitimate CodeGPT plugin, so matches need confirmation (pair with the C2-egress UC). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/06/marketplace-ecosystem-security-update-malicious-ai-plugins/ • https://hackread.com/malicious-jetbrains-plugins-steal-deepseek-openai-api-keys/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The legitimate 'CodeGPT' plugin (genuine vendor) whose folder name substring overlaps the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' clone
  • Developers who installed an affected plugin before JetBrains' takedown and have since updated/removed it (stale on-disk artifact)
  • Security team deliberately installing a sample for analysis in a lab VM
  • JetBrains Marketplace cache/temp extraction folders retaining the plugin name after backend disable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Marketplace\\cache\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact plugin ID inside the matched folder's plugin.xml against the 15 known IDs (e.g. org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit) — this disambiguates the malicious 'CodeGPT AI Assistant' from the legitimate CodeGPT. 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin, and immediately revoke/rotate any OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API key the developer may have entered (assume compromised even without observed egress). 3) Hunt: pivot every matched host to the C2-egress and HTTP-path UCs for 39.107.60.51 to confirm exfiltration, and query software inventory across the fleet for the remaining plugin IDs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20)
          by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    "DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs",
    "DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding",
    "AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI",
    "AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant",
    "DeepSeek AI Assist","Coding Simple Tool")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Google Vertex AI SDK Flaw Let Attackers Hijack Model Uploads via Bucket Squatting

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 9 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A flaw in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python let an attacker with no access to a victim's project hijack the victim's machine learning model upload and run code inside Google's serving infrastructure. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which found and reported the bug through Google's bug bounty program, calls the technique "Pickle in the Middle" and said it saw no exploitation in the wild.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Creation of GCS bucket matching predictable Vertex AI staging naming convention · [LLM] Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK (<1.148.0) install detected in pipeline/build
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI model registered with artifact URI in untrusted predictable staging bucket · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vertex AI model registered with artifact URI in untrusted predictable staging bucket AIDelivery Medium
Hunts Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel/UpdateModel audit events whose model artifact lives in a GCS bucket matching the SDK's predictable 'project-vertex-staging-region' naming convention. In the 'Pickle in the Middle' attack the victim SDK silently stages the model in an attacker-squatted bucket of that exact form, so a model whose source URI references a vertex-staging bucket not owned by the project is a direct indicator of upload hijack / model poisoning. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact predictable bucket form 'project-vertex-staging-region' (corroborated verbatim by Unit 42 and CSO Online) and the Vertex AI UploadModel control-plane call. The artifact URI is the one part of the cross-tenant hijack that is logged in the victim's own project (aiplatform.googleapis.com), making it the only victim-side detectable artifact. Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: Vertex AI model-registry audit events are GCP-native and do not land in Defender XDR, the provided Sentinel standard tables, Falcon FDR, or CloudWatch. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186193/googles-vertex-ai-sdk-could-allow-rce-through-bucket-squatting.html • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wh2j-26j7-9728
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1565.001 T1537
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teams that explicitly set staging_bucket to a shared bucket they legitimately own that happens to contain 'vertex-staging'
  • Central-ML-project architectures where models are intentionally staged cross-project
  • Patched SDK 1.148+ auto-created staging buckets carrying a uuid4 suffix (e.g. vertex-staging-<uuid>)
  • Third-party MLOps platforms registering models from their own managed GCS buckets
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(coalesce(object_path,command), "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}")  // drop patched-SDK uuid4-suffixed buckets
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the UploadModel event, extract the artifact bucket name and run `gsutil ls -L -b gs://<bucket>` / check Resource Manager to confirm which project OWNS that bucket; if the owning project is outside your org, treat as confirmed hijack. 2) Contain: undeploy/delete the affected Model and any Endpoints serving it, rotate the Vertex AI service-agent credentials, and revoke OAuth tokens issued to the serving container; block the foreign bucket. 3) Hunt: review all Models registered since the SDK was last unpatched (<1.148.0) for vertex-staging artifact URIs, and check serving-container egress for metadata-server token theft.

Creation of GCS bucket matching predictable Vertex AI staging naming convention AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts storage.buckets.create audit events for buckets matching the Vertex AI SDK's predictable 'project-vertex-staging-region' pattern without the post-patch uuid4 suffix. Defensively this surfaces internal/compromised accounts pre-creating squattable buckets and inventories predictable-name buckets in your own org that are hijack targets for the Pickle in the Middle technique. Rationale: Uses the article's literal predictable bucket form 'project-vertex-staging-region' as the match string and the GCS control-plane storage.buckets.create event. Because the attacker's bucket is created in the attacker's project (not visible to the victim), this is explicitly framed as org-internal hygiene / insider-squatting detection — high FP for orgs still on the pre-1.148 SDK whose legitimate clients auto-create the same name. Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: GCS admin-activity audit logs are GCP-native and absent from those platforms' provided schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1583.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pre-1.148 Vertex AI SDK legitimately auto-creating the default staging bucket for a fresh project+region (expected, high volume)
  • Data scientists manually creating staging buckets following the documented convention
  • Terraform / Deployment Manager IaC provisioning Vertex staging buckets
  • Patched 1.148+ SDK creating uuid4-suffixed vertex-staging buckets (filtered below)
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(object, "vertex-staging-[a-z0-9]{8}-[a-z0-9]{4}-[a-z0-9]{4}") AND NOT match(user, "service-.*@gcp-sa-aiplatform\.iam\.gserviceaccount\.com")  // drop uuid4-suffixed patched buckets and the Vertex service agent
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the creating principal (principalEmail) and project; confirm whether the bucket name lacks a uuid4 suffix (=created by vulnerable SDK or by hand) and whether the creator is a human/CI account vs the gcp-sa-aiplatform service agent. 2) Contain: if created by an unexpected/foreign or recently-compromised principal, lock the bucket, and force-set an explicit org-owned staging_bucket in affected pipelines so the SDK stops resolving predictable names. 3) Hunt: enumerate all vertex-staging buckets across the org, verify ownership, and upgrade every google-cloud-aiplatform install to >=1.148.0 (see SDK-version UC).

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK (<1.148.0) install detected in pipeline/build AIWeaponization High
Alerts on process-creation events showing installation of google-cloud-aiplatform pinned to a version below the patched 1.148.0 release (covers the article's tested-vulnerable 1.139.0/1.140.0 and the pre-fix 1.13x-1.147 range, plus the related CVE-2026-2473 <1.133.0). These versions resolve staging buckets by predictable name without ownership verification, exposing model uploads to bucket-squatting hijack. Rationale: Anchored on the exact patched/vulnerable version boundary the article and Google's advisory state: 1.139.0/1.140.0 tested-vulnerable, full fix in 1.148.0. The regex/version list deliberately matches 1.13x and 1.140-1.147 only, so patched 1.148+ does NOT fire — eliminating the biggest FP source. CloudWatch left empty (endpoint/CI telemetry, not AWS CloudTrail); the version range also covers the corroborated CVE-2026-2473 (<1.133.0) Experiments variant. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wh2j-26j7-9728 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/google-cloud-aiplatform/CVE-2026-2473/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally pinning an old SDK in a sandbox that never calls Model.upload()
  • Requirements-file installs (pip install -r) where the version is in the file, not the command line (detection gap, not a true FP)
  • Mirror/cache warming jobs that pre-download multiple historical versions
  • Reproducible-research environments deliberately frozen to an older version with an explicit org-owned staging_bucket already set
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/CI runner and whether the install feeds a pipeline that calls Model.upload() without an explicit staging_bucket; check whether google-cloud-aiplatform is actually the resolved runtime version (pip show). 2) Contain: upgrade to >=1.148.0 in the affected requirements/lockfile and rebuild the image; set an explicit org-owned staging_bucket in all upload code paths. 3) Hunt: sweep notebooks, CI jobs, and container layers org-wide for the same pinned versions, then pivot to the model-upload-URI and bucket-creation UCs to confirm no hijack already occurred while unpatched.

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",

| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",

                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 19 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged multiple ClickFix campaigns that deliver three malware loaders called BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and Potemkin, per independent reports from Morphisec, BlueVoyant, and Huntress, respectively. Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix initial access: explorer-spawned shell download cradle pulling ZIP / Node.js · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Lorem Ipsum Loader: legacy Node.js 7.10.1 executing JS payload from user-writable path · [LLM] Lorem Ipsum Loader: DLL side-load of mscoree.dll / msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path · [LLM] Potemkin loader: victim-UUID marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver · [LLM] Potemkin delivery: msiexec spawning mshta (MSI → HTA loader drop) · [LLM] BabaDeda Storage Crypter: external payload container List.Control.dat · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ClickFix loader C2: node.exe outbound beacon from user-writable path · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Lorem Ipsum Loader: legacy Node.js 7.10.1 executing JS payload from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the Lorem Ipsum (Vanilla Tempest/Rapid Brigantine) ClickFix chain that downloads an outdated 2017 Node.js runtime (v7.10.1) alongside a ZIP, then uses node.exe to run JavaScript droppers while evading detection. Article-specific because legitimate enterprise software ships current Node, not v7.10.1 launched from Temp/AppData. Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete strings: node.exe + Node.js version 7.10.1 + JS execution from user-writable directories. Confirmed by BlueVoyant and DarkReading as the Lorem Ipsum ClickFix delivery runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/lorem-ipsum-malware-clickfix-delivery
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations running an intentionally pinned old Node.js for legacy build tooling
  • Electron apps bundling node.exe under AppData running internal .js
  • npm global scripts executing from %AppData%\Roaming\npm
  • CI/build agents launching node from a temp checkout directory
  • VS Code / language servers spawning node from AppData\Local\Programs
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Roaming\npm\", @"\AppData\Local\Yarn\", @"\AppData\Roaming\nvm\", @"\AppData\Local\fnm\", @"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion — v7.10.1 from Temp/AppData is near-certain malicious; pull the .js path and parent (explorer/powershell). 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the node.exe tree, capture the ZIP and JS dropper for analysis, block any C2 reached. 3) Hunt: Search same host/user for mscoree.dll/msvcp140.dll side-loads, batch persistence, and downstream Rhysida pre-encryption activity across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".js", ".cjs", ".mjs")
| where ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7.10.1"
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (".js", ".cjs", ".mjs")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Legacy Node.js Runtime Executing Script From User-Writable Path (Lorem Ipsum Loader)
id: 7c3e1a92-4b6d-4f2a-9e15-2a9c8d4f1b03
description: Detects node.exe running a JavaScript file from a temp/AppData/Downloads location, matching the Lorem Ipsum ClickFix chain that ships an outdated Node.js 7.10.1 to execute JS droppers.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
  - https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
  selection_script:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.js'
      - '.cjs'
      - '.mjs'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains:
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Public\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection_img and selection_script and selection_path
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE) (@CommandLine:*.js* OR @CommandLine:*.cjs* OR @CommandLine:*.mjs*) (@Image:*\Temp\* OR @Image:*\AppData\* OR @Image:*\Downloads\* OR @Image:*\Public\* OR @Image:*\ProgramData\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\.(js|cjs|mjs)/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(Temp|AppData|Downloads|Public|ProgramData)\\/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="node.exe" AND (Processes.process="*.js*" OR Processes.process="*.cjs*" OR Processes.process="*.mjs*") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="node.exe" AND (Processes.process="*.js*" OR Processes.process="*.cjs*" OR Processes.process="*.mjs*") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Lorem Ipsum Loader: DLL side-load of mscoree.dll / msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Lorem Ipsum batch-persistence chain that side-loads a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll to decode the loader payload. These are legitimate Microsoft DLLs that normally live in System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS — loading from Temp/AppData by a process in the same location indicates side-loading. Rationale: Uses the article's named side-loaded DLLs (mscoree.dll, msvcp140.dll) plus the abnormal-location heuristic. Morphisec/BlueVoyant confirm DLL side-loading as the loader-decode mechanism in this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/what-is-the-babadeda-loader-analysis-of-a-new-clickfix-malware-campaign/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/standalone .NET apps carrying their own mscoree.dll in a user folder
  • Sideloaded enterprise line-of-business apps under AppData\Local\Programs
  • Microsoft Teams/Discord/Slack/Zoom bundling msvcp140.dll under AppData
  • Software installers staging runtime DLLs in %TEMP% during setup
  • Game launchers shipping VC++ runtime DLLs in their own ProgramData dir
Suppression filter

Potemkin loader: victim-UUID marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the Potemkin loader's victim-identification file 'hyper-v.ver' under Local AppData, used to write a unique UUID per infected host. The filename masquerades as a Hyper-V artifact; genuine Hyper-V does not write this file to a user profile. Rationale: Single high-fidelity string straight from the article and corroborated by Huntress/gbhackers: '%LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver' as the Potemkin victim-UUID file. Effectively zero legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/potemkin-loader-rmmproject-clickfix-attack • https://gbhackers.com/clickfix-attack-deploys-potemkin-loader/
ATT&CKT1082 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no known legitimate software writes hyper-v.ver to a user AppData path
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonation of the sample in-house
  • Backup or DLP agent re-creating a previously quarantined sample file
  • EDR test/purple-team replay of the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: Treat any hit as high-confidence Potemkin; read the writing process and the UUID contents, and capture the loader binary. 2) Contain: Isolate host, kill the loader process, block its resolved DGA C2, preserve memory (modules load reflectively in-memory). 3) Hunt: Pivot on the writing process to find the parent MSI/HTA chain, look for RMMProject/EtherRAT and browser-credential theft (ABE bypass), and sweep the org for the same filename.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Potemkin delivery: msiexec spawning mshta (MSI → HTA loader drop) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Potemkin initial chain where an installed MSI package spawns mshta.exe to drop the loader via an HTA payload. msiexec.exe directly launching mshta.exe is highly abnormal and matches the documented Potemkin/RMMProject/EtherRAT ClickFix intrusion. Rationale: Process-tree pivot from the article's described chain: MSI package -> HTA payload -> Potemkin loader. msiexec.exe -> mshta.exe is a rare, high-signal parent/child pair confirmed in the Huntress write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/potemkin-loader-rmmproject-clickfix-attack • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-clickfix-prompt-to-install-msi-package/amp/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise installers using a custom action that invokes mshta for a setup UI
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools (e.g., MSI authoring suites) testing HTA actions
  • Vendor installers showing an HTA-based EULA or progress dialog
  • Admin-built MSI wrappers that chain mshta for post-install config
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the MSI path/product name and the mshta command line / HTA URL or file; benign installers reference a local .hta, malicious ones often fetch remote content. 2) Contain: Isolate host, terminate the mshta tree, block the HTA source URL, quarantine the MSI. 3) Hunt: Look for the Potemkin marker hyper-v.ver, reflective module loads, DGA-style DNS bursts, and RMMProject browser-credential theft on the host and across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix loader C2: node.exe outbound beacon from user-writable path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts loader/EtherRAT C2 where node.exe (the Lorem Ipsum runtime and the EtherRAT Node.js backdoor) — running from Temp/AppData rather than Program Files — makes outbound connections to public IPs. Flags the article's candidate C2 IPs as enrichment without gating on them. Rationale: Behavioral C2 pivot tying the article's two Node.js-based families (Lorem Ipsum runtime, EtherRAT Node.js backdoor) to abnormal node.exe egress; the article's IPs (95.163.152.190, 91.92.243.161) are used only as enrichment flags because no second source confirmed them. Sentinel left empty: process-attributed network egress is not available on this tenant's ASIM tables (ImNetworkSession lacks an initiating-process field) without the MDE connector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine • https://gbhackers.com/clickfix-attack-deploys-potemkin-loader/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer node.exe reaching npm registry / GitHub / public APIs
  • Electron apps under AppData phoning home for updates/telemetry
  • Build agents pulling dependencies from public mirrors
  • Local dev servers proxying to public SaaS endpoints
  • node-based CLI tools (e.g., npx) hitting public CDNs
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Roaming\npm\", @"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\", @"\AppData\Local\Yarn\", @"\AppData\Roaming\nvm\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the node.exe path and command line; node from %TEMP%/%AppData% beaconing to a single public IP on an odd port is suspicious — check whether the destination matches the candidate C2 IPs. 2) Contain: Block the destination IP/domain, isolate host, kill node.exe. 3) Hunt: Correlate with node.exe execution of JS from ZIP (same host), check DNS for DGA bursts, and look for Lorem Ipsum backdoor next-stage downloads from social-media-hosted C2 profiles.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| extend KnownCandidateC2 = RemoteIP in ("95.163.152.190", "91.92.243.161")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, KnownCandidateC2
| order by KnownCandidateC2 desc, LastSeen desc

| order by KnownCandidateC2 desc, LastSeen desc

ClickFix initial access: explorer-spawned shell download cradle pulling ZIP / Node.js AIDelivery Medium
Detects the ClickFix social-engineering step where a user pastes an attacker-supplied command into the Run dialog, causing explorer.exe to spawn PowerShell/cmd/mshta that downloads the loader ZIP and legacy Node.js runtime. The explorer.exe parent + download cradle + .zip/node payload reference is the ClickFix signature for these campaigns. Rationale: Targets the article's ClickFix initial-access step (user runs attacker-supplied PowerShell that downloads a ZIP + Node.js). Anchored on explorer.exe (Run-dialog) parentage plus the campaign-specific .zip/node payload reference to differentiate from generic phishing-click and Office-spawn rules; confirmed by BlueVoyant and SecurityBrief. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine • https://securitybrief.com.au/story/rapid-brigantine-ties-clickfix-malware-to-fake-updates
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins pasting legitimate download one-liners into the Run box
  • Software deployment scripts launched manually via Run
  • Power users invoking curl/Invoke-WebRequest for legit .zip downloads
  • Help-desk remote-support tools fetching utilities
  • Developers running node bootstrap commands from Run
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-deploy", "admin-install")) and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm", "intune", "\\\\corp-share\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read the full command line — decode any URL and confirm the downloaded ZIP/node target; explorer.exe parent strongly implies Run-dialog paste (ClickFix). 2) Contain: Isolate host, kill the shell tree, block the download URL/host, quarantine any dropped ZIP/node. 3) Hunt: Follow on to node.exe JS execution, DLL side-loads (mscoree/msvcp140), hyper-v.ver/List.Control.dat artifacts, and downstream RAT/stealer C2; check whether the lure domain impersonates a vendor (Edge/Adobe/Microsoft update).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr", "curl", "Invoke-RestMethod", "Start-BitsTransfer", "DownloadFile", "DownloadString")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", "nodejs", ".js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://", "https://", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr", "curl", "DownloadFile", "DownloadString", "Start-BitsTransfer")
| where CommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", "nodejs", ".js")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"

title: ClickFix Run-Dialog Download Cradle Pulling ZIP or Node.js
id: c8a1d703-6f42-4b18-9d05-2e7a4c9b3f61
description: Detects explorer.exe spawning powershell/cmd/mshta with a network download primitive and a reference to a .zip or node payload, matching the ClickFix lure that delivers the BabaDeda/Lorem Ipsum loaders.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
  - https://www.bluevoyant.com/blog/orem-ipsum-clickfix-rapid-brigantine
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1204.001
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  selection_download:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'http://'
      - 'https://'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'Start-BitsTransfer'
      - 'curl'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.zip'
      - 'node'
      - '.js'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_download and selection_payload
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:*\explorer.exe OR @ParentImage:*\EXPLORER.EXE) (@Image:*\powershell.exe OR @Image:*\PowerShell.EXE OR @Image:*\pwsh.exe OR @Image:*\cmd.exe OR @Image:*\CMD.EXE OR @Image:*\mshta.exe OR @Image:*\MSHTA.EXE) (@CommandLine:*http* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-WebRequest* OR @CommandLine:*DownloadString* OR @CommandLine:*DownloadFile* OR @CommandLine:*Start-BitsTransfer* OR @CommandLine:*curl*) (@CommandLine:*.zip* OR @CommandLine:*node* OR @CommandLine:*.js*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|cmd|mshta)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(http|Invoke-WebRequest|DownloadString|DownloadFile|Start-BitsTransfer|curl)/i
| CommandLine=/(\.zip|node|\.js)/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Start-BitsTransfer*" OR Processes.process="*curl*") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" AND (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Start-BitsTransfer*" OR Processes.process="*curl*") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.js*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
